GICI4OS · OPERATING SYSTEMS · LAB 1

Exploring Operating System Basics

Lab 1 guide: Linux in brief, then find out which system you are on, practise the basic commands, and see programs and processes at work.

Heng Rathpisey · Department GIC · Academic year 2025–2026

Learning objectives

  1. Identify basic operating system and kernel information.
  2. Use essential Linux file and directory commands.
  3. Install, remove, and purge software using the APT package manager.
  4. Understand the difference between a program and a running process.
  5. Observe multitasking in a running operating system.
  6. Detect whether an operating system is running on a virtualized environment.

THIS LAB

Lab 1

First, Linux in brief. Then Part A in class, on the course server, and Part B as homework, on your own Ubuntu.

Lab 1 · 02

DISCUSSION

You log in to a server you have never seen. What do you check first?

Which system it is, what is in your folder, and what is running. This lab shows you how to find out.

Lab 1 · 03

LINUX IN BRIEF

What is Linux, and why learn it?

Where it comes from, how a distribution is built, and how you talk to it.

Lab 1 · 04

Linux is everywhere

  • Servers and cloud platforms
  • Android phones and tablets, which use the Linux kernel
  • Routers, smart TVs and cars
  • Supercomputers
  • Developers' laptops and desktops

As an engineer you will meet Linux again and again. That is why this course works on it.

Linux in brief · 05

Where Linux comes from

  • Linus Torvalds developed the first version, 0.01, in 1991.
  • Linux was first distributed as source code only.
  • Later it came as a pair of downloadable floppy-disk images.
  • One image was bootable and held the Linux kernel.
  • The other held a set of GNU utilities and tools for setting up a file system.

Linus Torvalds, 1969 to present

Linux in brief · 06

The Linux kernel

  • The kernel is the core of the operating system.
  • It manages the processor, the memory and the devices.
  • Programs ask it for services through system calls.
  • Linux is the kernel. A distribution adds the programs around it.

Linux in brief · 07

A Linux distribution, or distro

An operating system made from a software collection, based on the Linux kernel and, often, a package management system.

A typical distribution comprises

  • A Linux kernel
  • GNU tools
  • Others: libraries, additional software, documentation, a window system, a window manager and a desktop environment

Desktop and applications

window system, window manager, desktop environment

GNU tools and libraries

Linux kernel

what Linus Torvalds started

Hardware

About 500 to 600 distributions are in active development (the figure given in the earlier Lab 1 guide).

Linux in brief · 08

Layers of a Linux distribution

Programs in user mode sit on the kernel, and the kernel sits on the hardware.

Linux in brief · 09

A timeline of distributions

Each line is one distribution. Most of them branch from an older one.

Linux in brief · 10

Linux families

FamilyExamplesPackage filesTools
DebianDebian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint, Raspberry Pi OS.debdpkg, apt
Red HatRed Hat Enterprise Linux, Fedora, CentOS.rpmrpm, yum, dnf
SUSESUSE Linux Enterprise, openSUSE.rpmrpm, zypper
SlackwareSlackware.tgzpkgtools

This lab uses Ubuntu, so you use the tools of the Debian family: dpkg and apt.

Linux in brief · 11

The families over time

Debian, Slackware, SUSE and Red Hat each started a family of distributions.

Linux in brief · 12

Package management

01

Packages

A distribution is normally split into packages. Each package holds one application or service.

02

What a package holds

The software, and metadata: its full name, a description of its purpose, a version number, a checksum, and the list of dependencies it needs to run.

03

The package manager

A collection of tools that automates installing, upgrading, configuring and removing programs, in a consistent way.

A dependency is another package that this one needs.

Linux in brief · 13

DPKG

DPKG is the package manager of Debian-based systems.

It can install, remove and build packages. Unlike other package managers, it cannot download and install packages or their dependencies by itself.

Details: man dpkg

student@ubuntu: ~

$ dpkg -l                 # list all installed packages

$ dpkg -l | grep xxx      # check if xxx is installed

$ sudo dpkg -i xxx.deb    # install xxx.deb

$ sudo dpkg -r xxx        # uninstall xxx

Linux in brief · 14

APT

The apt command works with Ubuntu's Advanced Packaging Tool.

It installs new packages, upgrades the ones you have, updates the package list, and can even upgrade the whole system.

Details: apt help. Lab 1 uses apt-get, the older command with the same actions.

student@ubuntu: ~

$ sudo apt install xxx    # install xxx

$ sudo apt remove xxx     # remove xxx

$ sudo apt update         # update the local package index

$ sudo apt upgrade        # update packages and system

Linux in brief · 15

Why is knowing the command line important?

Flexibility and mobility.

  • When you understand the foundation of Linux, you can work on any Linux distribution.
  • That may be one company with a mixed environment.
  • Or a new company that uses a different distribution.
  • Many servers have no graphical desktop at all.

Linux in brief · 16

What is a shell?

You

type a command

The terminal

takes what you typed and passes it on

The shell

the command-line interpreter, here bash

The operating system

carries out the action

The terminal

Once you have entered a command, the terminal accepts what you typed and passes it to a shell.

The shell

The shell is the command-line interpreter. It translates the commands you enter into actions to be performed by the operating system.

Linux in brief · 17

The prompt

When a terminal starts, the shell shows a prompt. Its structure varies between distributions, but it typically tells you about the user and the system.

User name

terminal

sysadmin@localhost:~$

System name

terminal

sysadmin@localhost:~$

Current directory

terminal

sysadmin@localhost:~$

The $ at the end means you are a normal user, and the shell is waiting for your command.

Linux in brief · 18

The ~ symbol is your home directory

sysadmin@localhost: ~

sysadmin@localhost:~$ pwd

/home/sysadmin

sysadmin@localhost:~$ cd /etc

sysadmin@localhost:/etc$ pwd

/etc

sysadmin@localhost:/etc$ cd ~

sysadmin@localhost:~$ pwd

/home/sysadmin

The ~ symbol is shorthand for the user's home directory.

Watch the prompt: it shows ~ while you are at home, and the real path when you are somewhere else.

cd ~ brings you home from anywhere.

Lab 1 · 31

Where does the output of a command go?

Normally: to the screen

ls

a command

its output

the standard output

the screen

you read it, then it is gone

With > or >>: into a file

ls > list.txt

the same command, redirected

its output

the standard output

list.txt

it is saved, and the screen shows nothing

This is called output redirection. You use it in every task to keep a record of your results.

Lab 1 · 32

The syntax of > and >>

You typeWhat it meansIf the file is newIf the file exists
COMMAND > FILESend the output into FILEFILE is createdIts old content is replaced
COMMAND >> FILEAdd the output to the end of FILEFILE is createdIts old content stays, and the new output comes after it

One arrow replaces

Think of > as: start this file again.

Two arrows add

Think of >> as: write on the next line.

The command does not change

Only where its output goes changes. COMMAND can be any command.

Lab 1 · 33

See the difference

> replaces the file

one arrow

$ echo one > a.txt

$ echo two > a.txt

$ cat a.txt

two

>> adds to the end

two arrows

$ echo one > a.txt

$ echo two >> a.txt

$ cat a.txt

one

two

In this lab the first line of a record file uses > and every later line uses >>.

Lab 1 · 39

TASK 4

Program or process?

A program is a file. A process is a program that is running.

Lab 1 · 40

A program stays. A process comes and goes.

Program file

sleep: a file on the disk

Process

sleep 30 &

which sleep finds the file before, during and after. ps shows a sleep line only while the process runs.

Lab 1 · 41

Run it in the background

student@server: ~/oslab-work/lab1

$ which sleep

$ sleep 30 &

$ ps > task4_process_list.txt

$ cat task4_process_list.txt

thirty seconds later

$ ps

$ which sleep

  • The & at the end runs the command in the background and gives you the prompt back.
  • ps lists the processes of your terminal.
  • Afterwards ps shows no sleep, but which sleep still finds the file.

For your report: what did you see before, during and after?

Lab 1 · 49

Why is there a checkpoint?

It shows what you can do alone

For most of the lab you may use hints and AI tools. The checkpoint is the one moment without them. It tells you, and the instructor, which commands you really know.

Your numbers are new

The names and numbers change at the checkpoint. An answer copied from a neighbour, or from your own earlier output, does not fit.

The instructor sees who needs help

Your answers arrive at once. The instructor can explain a common mistake before the next lab builds on this one.

It is fair

Everyone gets the same kind of task. You can take it even if an earlier task is not finished.

Lab 1 · Part B · 58

Task 3: what each command does

CommandWhat it does
sudo apt-get updateRefreshes the list of available software. Installs nothing.
sudo apt-get install mcDownloads and installs the package.
sudo apt-get remove mcUninstalls the program. Keeps its settings in /etc.
sudo apt-get purge mcUninstalls the program and deletes its settings.

mc is Midnight Commander. Its settings live in the folder /etc/mc.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat happensFix
Typing FILE1 literallyA file named FILE1.txt appearsUse your own file1 from oslab values lab1
> instead of >>The record keeps only the last lineUse >> after the first line
Forgetting the &The terminal waits and you cannot typePress Ctrl+C, run it again with &
Running ps too lateThere is no sleep lineRun ps right after you start sleep
Working in the wrong folderNo such file or directoryCheck with pwd and ls

Lab 1 · 66

Key takeaways

01

Kernel and distribution

Linux is the kernel. Ubuntu is the kernel plus many other programs.

02

Program and process

A program is a file. A process is a running copy of it.

03

Remove and purge

Remove keeps the settings in /etc. Purge deletes them.

04

One arrow or two

> replaces a file. >> adds to its end.
